questionMappings.question: What role does the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) play in CPython?

options.text: It compiles Python code directly into machine code before execution
It is a mutex ensuring only one native thread executes Python bytecode at a time, protecting CPython memory management
It prevents all multi-threaded programming in Python completely
It automatically optimizes I/O bound operations by bypassing the operating system

questionMappings.explanation: CPython uses reference counting which is not thread-safe. The GIL ensures only one thread executes Python bytecode at once, meaning CPU-bound multi-threading requires multiprocessing instead.

questionMappings.question: What is the Method Resolution Order (MRO) algorithm used in modern Python 3 multiple inheritance?

options.text: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
Depth-First Search (DFS)
Dijkstra Priority Queue
C3 Linearization

questionMappings.explanation: Python uses the C3 Linearization algorithm to determine a deterministic order for resolving method calls in complex multiple inheritance hierarchies.

questionMappings.question: What is the average time complexity of checking membership `x in s` for a Python set vs a Python list of length N?

options.text: Set: O(log N), List: O(1)
Set: O(N log N), List: O(N)
Set: O(N), List: O(N)
Set: O(1), List: O(N)

questionMappings.explanation: Python sets are implemented as hash tables offering average O(1) key lookup, whereas lists require linear search scanning elements sequentially with O(N) complexity.

questionMappings.question: What happens in the following try-except-finally block?

options.text: 10 is printed
20 is printed
SyntaxError: multiple return statements in same scope
30 is printed

questionMappings.explanation: The finally block is guaranteed to execute before the function exits. When a return statement is encountered inside finally, it overwrites any previous return value from try or except.

questionMappings.question: What is the output of this Python code regarding mutable default arguments?
questionMappings.codeSnippet:
def append_item(val, items=[]):
    items.append(val)
    return items

print(append_item(1))
print(append_item(2))

options.text: [1] followed by [2]
TypeError: mutable default argument not permitted
[1, 2] followed by [1, 2]
[1] followed by [1, 2]

questionMappings.explanation: In Python, default arguments are evaluated once when the function definition is executed, meaning the same list instance is reused across invocations unless explicitly re-instantiated.

questionMappings.question: In Python, what is the purpose of the `copy.deepcopy()` function compared to `copy.copy()`?

options.text: deepcopy recursively copies all objects found inside compound objects, preventing mutations in the clone from affecting the original
copy.copy clones nested compound objects recursively, while deepcopy only copies references
deepcopy creates a C-level pointer to the original memory block
deepcopy encrypts the object into byte memory

questionMappings.explanation: A shallow copy constructs a new compound object but inserts references to the original nested objects. deepcopy recursively duplicates all child objects.

questionMappings.question: What is the primary difference between a Python generator and a regular function returning a list?

options.text: Generators yield items lazily on demand, saving memory compared to eagerly constructing an entire list in RAM
Generators automatically convert all returned values to JSON strings
Generators cannot accept arguments or maintain local state
Generators execute in a separate operating system thread

questionMappings.explanation: Generators use the yield keyword to produce values lazily one at a time via the iterator protocol, resulting in O(1) space complexity instead of O(N) memory allocation.

questionMappings.question: What does the `@classmethod` decorator do in Python?

options.text: Converts a method to a static method that takes no arguments
Automatically instantiates a new class object upon invocation
Makes the method private and accessible only within the defining module
Passes the class itself (cls) as the first argument instead of the instance (self)

questionMappings.explanation: A @classmethod receives the class object as its first argument (conventionally named cls), allowing factory constructors and class-level state modifications.

questionMappings.question: What is the CSS specificity hierarchy from highest to lowest priority?

options.text: All selectors have identical specificity weight
Element -> Class -> ID -> Inline style
Inline style -> ID selector -> Class/Attribute/Pseudo-class -> Element selector
Class -> ID -> Element -> Inline style

questionMappings.explanation: Inline styles (1,0,0,0) override ID selectors (0,1,0,0), which override class/pseudo-classes (0,0,1,0), which override element selectors (0,0,0,1).

questionMappings.question: What CSS unit is relative to the font-size of the root `<html>` element?

options.text: vh
ch
em
rem

questionMappings.explanation: rem stands for "root em" and scales relative to the root html font-size (typically 16px by default), unlike em which scales relative to the immediate parent font-size.

questionMappings.question: What is the purpose of the `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">` tag in HTML?

options.text: Enables dark mode automatically
Instructs mobile browsers to match screen width and sets initial zoom level for responsive rendering
Preloads all CSS stylesheets
Enables 3D hardware acceleration in mobile browsers

questionMappings.explanation: Without the viewport meta tag, mobile browsers assume a desktop viewport (~980px) and scale down content, breaking responsive media queries.

questionMappings.question: Which CSS property creates a two-dimensional grid layout capable of handling both rows and columns simultaneously?

options.text: display: table
display: flex
display: grid
display: inline-block

questionMappings.explanation: CSS Grid is designed for 2D layouts (rows and columns simultaneously), whereas Flexbox is primarily designed for 1D layouts (a single row or column at a time).

questionMappings.question: What does the CSS property `flex-wrap: wrap` do in a Flexbox container?

options.text: Reverses the order of flex items
Allows flex items to break onto multiple lines if they exceed container width instead of overflowing or squishing
Shrinks all items to zero width
Aligns items vertically in the center

questionMappings.explanation: By default, flex-wrap is nowrap which forces all items onto a single line. Setting wrap allows elements to wrap gracefully onto subsequent lines.

questionMappings.question: What is the difference between `box-sizing: content-box` and `box-sizing: border-box` in CSS?

options.text: border-box only works on table elements
content-box renders elements without margins
border-box includes padding and border within the specified width and height, whereas content-box adds them on top of the dimensions
border-box excludes borders from the element calculation

questionMappings.explanation: With border-box, an element with width: 200px and 20px padding remains 200px wide. With content-box, the total rendered width becomes 240px.

questionMappings.question: What creates a new Stacking Context in CSS affecting `z-index` layering?

options.text: Any paragraph element
Positioned elements with z-index, opacity less than 1, transform properties, or filter effects
Adding a class attribute to an element
Setting font-size to 14px

questionMappings.explanation: A stacking context is a 3D conceptualization of HTML elements. Once formed, child z-index values are contained and cannot break out relative to parent siblings.

questionMappings.question: How does `position: sticky` behave in CSS?

options.text: It acts as `relative` until a specified scroll threshold is reached, then sticks like `fixed` within its parent container
It animates smoothly to the center of the screen
It positions an element relative to the entire screen viewport at all times
It prevents the element from being clicked

questionMappings.explanation: sticky toggles between relative and fixed positioning based on the user scroll position, constrained within the bounds of its parent container.

questionMappings.question: Which header file must be included to use malloc() and free() in C?

options.text: <stdio.h>
<stdlib.h>
<memory.h>
<string.h>

questionMappings.explanation: <stdlib.h> contains the function prototypes for dynamic memory allocation functions malloc, calloc, realloc, and free.

questionMappings.question: What happens if you allocate dynamic memory with `malloc()` but never call `free()` before program exit?

options.text: A segmentation fault occurs immediately
The memory is automatically freed by the C runtime garbage collector
A memory leak occurs during execution; operating systems reclaim the virtual address space upon process termination
The compiler issues a fatal syntax error

questionMappings.explanation: Failing to free heap memory causes a memory leak that consumes RAM during program runtime. While modern OSes clean up process memory on exit, long-running services will exhaust system memory.

questionMappings.question: What is a "dangling pointer" in C programming?

options.text: A pointer that has not yet been declared
A pointer that points to a memory location that has already been deallocated
A pointer initialized to NULL
A pointer stored in read-only code segment

questionMappings.explanation: A dangling pointer references memory that has been freed. Dereferencing it leads to undefined behavior or security vulnerabilities.

questionMappings.question: What is the correct format specifier for printing an unsigned integer using printf?

options.text: %u
%d
%i
%f

questionMappings.explanation: %u is specifically designated for printing unsigned decimal integers in C.

questionMappings.question: What character is automatically appended to string literals to indicate their end in C?

options.text: 'EOF'

questionMappings.explanation: C strings are null-terminated character arrays ending with the null terminator character '\0' (ASCII 0).

questionMappings.question: What does the sizeof operator return in C?

options.text: Size in bytes as a size_t
Number of memory addresses allocated
Length of string excluding null character
Size in bits

questionMappings.explanation: sizeof returns the memory size of an expression or type in bytes, represented as size_t.

questionMappings.question: What is the output of pointer arithmetic when incrementing `ptr++` where `int *ptr = 1000;` on a 64-bit system where `sizeof(int) == 4`?

options.text: Undefined behavior

questionMappings.explanation: In C, incrementing a typed pointer increases its address by sizeof(T) bytes. Since sizeof(int) is 4, 1000 + 4 = 1004.

questionMappings.question: What does the `static` keyword mean when applied to a global variable in a C source file (.c)?

options.text: The variable cannot be modified (constant)
The variable is stored on the stack frame
The variable is dynamically allocated at runtime
The variable has internal linkage, meaning it is only visible within that compilation unit

questionMappings.explanation: When used at file scope, static gives the symbol internal linkage, preventing other translation units from linking or referencing it directly.

questionMappings.question: What is a "dangling pointer" in C?

options.text: An uninitialized pointer pointing to arbitrary memory
A pointer pointing to a memory location that has already been deallocated
A pointer that points to NULL
A pointer declared inside a recursive function

questionMappings.explanation: A dangling pointer arises when memory pointed to by a pointer has been freed, but the pointer was not reset to NULL.

questionMappings.question: What is structure padding in C?

options.text: Adding empty string fields to structs
Compiler insertion of unused bytes between structure members to satisfy hardware memory alignment requirements
Encrypting structure data in memory
Reserving memory for future struct expansion

questionMappings.explanation: Processors access memory more efficiently in 4-byte or 8-byte aligned words; compilers pad structures to align member offsets.

questionMappings.question: Why do C compilers add padding bytes between struct members?

options.text: To leave space for object-oriented virtual method tables
To satisfy hardware memory alignment requirements for efficient CPU bus access
To prevent buffer overflow exploits
To encrypt struct data in memory

questionMappings.explanation: Modern CPU architectures access memory faster when multi-byte data types are aligned to addresses that are multiples of their size. Compilers insert padding to ensure proper data alignment.

questionMappings.question: What character marks the end of a valid C-string in memory?

options.text: Null character '\0' (ASCII 0)
Character '/n'
Character '$'
EOF marker

questionMappings.explanation: C strings are null-terminated byte sequences where the character '\0' denotes the end of the string. Functions like strlen() scan until reaching this byte.

questionMappings.question: What happens when you pass an array to a function in C?

options.text: The function receives the array length automatically as a hidden argument
Compilation fails unless passed by reference using the & operator
The array decays into a pointer to its first element
A complete deep copy of the array elements is created on the call stack

questionMappings.explanation: In C, array names decay into a pointer to the type of their first element when passed as function arguments.

questionMappings.question: What is the difference between `malloc()` and `calloc()`?

options.text: calloc() initializes the allocated memory to all zero bits; malloc() leaves memory uninitialized
calloc() allocates stack memory; malloc() allocates heap memory
malloc() automatically frees memory when out of scope
calloc() can only allocate memory for char pointers

questionMappings.explanation: calloc(num, size) zeroes out all allocated memory bytes and checks for integer overflow in the size calculation. malloc(size) leaves the memory contents indeterminate.

questionMappings.question: What does realloc(ptr, 0) do in standard compliant modern C (C23)?

options.text: Allocates a zero-length array
Doubles the allocated buffer
Has undefined or deallocating behavior; modern C standard deprecates or treats zero size as freeing ptr or returning NULL
Throws a BadAllocException

questionMappings.explanation: Calling realloc with size 0 is historically undefined/inconsistent and in modern standards frees the memory or returns NULL.

questionMappings.question: What does the `volatile` type qualifier tell the C compiler?

options.text: The variable can be modified by hardware or concurrent threads, disabling compiler caching/optimization into CPU registers
The variable must be cleared when a function returns
The variable is thread-safe and atomic
The variable will be stored on external persistent storage

questionMappings.explanation: `volatile` tells the compiler never to optimize away reads or writes to the variable, ensuring every read/write hits actual memory.

questionMappings.question: What is the bitwise result of `5 & 3` in C?
questionMappings.explanation: 5 in binary is 0101; 3 in binary is 0011. Performing bitwise AND (0101 & 0011) results in 0001, which is 1.

questionMappings.question: What is Undefined Behavior (UB) in C?

options.text: Code execution for which the ISO C standard imposes no requirements, allowing crashes, corrupted data, or erratic behavior
Platform-dependent behavior with documented implementation choices
An error reported during compilation with code -1
A syntax error caught by linting tools

questionMappings.explanation: Undefined behavior occurs when code violates standard rules (like buffer overflow or dereferencing null); compilers make no guarantees about execution.

questionMappings.question: What is the danger of using `gets()` in C, which led to its complete removal in C11?

options.text: It cannot read strings containing spaces
It is too slow compared to scanf
It does not perform boundary checks on the destination buffer, allowing catastrophic buffer overflow vulnerabilities
It fails to convert uppercase to lowercase

questionMappings.explanation: gets() has no mechanism to limit the number of characters read, meaning user input exceeding the destination buffer will overwrite adjacent stack memory, enabling arbitrary code execution.

questionMappings.question: How can you prevent multiple inclusion of header files in C?

Using static inline declarations
Using preprocessor include guards (#ifndef HEADER_H ... #endif) or #pragma once
Compiling with the -no-duplicate flag

questionMappings.explanation: Include guards (#ifndef, #define, #endif) prevent compiler errors caused by re-declaring types when a header is included multiple times.
